title: Spanish Article Mistakes: When to Use El, La, Un and Una

meta_description: Spanish article mistakes learners make: el for general nouns, no un with jobs, otro, medio, cien, days, titles and body parts, with fixes and a quiz.
excerpt: When Spanish adds an article English leaves out, and when it drops one English needs.

body_html:
Spanish article mistakes are subtle but constant, because Spanish and English use articles in different places. Spanish adds el or la where English uses nothing (Me gusta el café, “I like coffee”), and drops un or una where English needs “a” (Soy profesora, “I’m a teacher”). None of these errors block understanding, but together they make your Spanish sound translated. Here are the patterns that matter most.

Key takeaways
  • Use the definite article for nouns in a general sense: La vida es bella.
  • Drop un/una with professions, nationalities and religions after ser: Es médico.
  • Never say un otro, un medio, un cien or un mil.
  • Use el with days, titles and body parts: el lunes, el señor Pérez, me duele la cabeza.
{{toc}}

Spanish article mistakes with general nouns

English drops the article when talking about something in general: “Coffee is expensive”, “I love music”. Spanish keeps it:

  • El café está caro. Coffee is expensive.
  • Me encanta la música. I love music.
  • Los perros son leales. Dogs are loyal.
  • La paciencia es importante. Patience is important.

This is especially frequent with gustar-type verbs: Me gustan los libros, never Me gustan libros. See {{link:how-to-use-gustar|how to use gustar}}. The RAE’s Nueva gramática describes this generic use of the definite article in detail.

No un with professions, nationalities and religions

After ser, Spanish usually drops the indefinite article before an unmodified noun of profession, nationality, religion or similar category:

  • Soy abogada. I’m a lawyer.
  • Mi padre es ingeniero. My father is an engineer.
  • Es mexicano. He’s Mexican.

Add the article back when there is an adjective: Es un médico excelente (He’s an excellent doctor).

What a day!¡Qué un día!¡Qué día!
{{image:2}}

Days, times and dates

  • El lunes voy al médico. On Monday I’m going to the doctor.
  • Los sábados juego al fútbol. On Saturdays I play soccer.
  • Son las tres. It’s three o’clock.
  • El 5 de mayo. On the 5th of May.

No preposition is needed: el lunes, not en el lunes. See {{link:spanish-preposition-mistakes|Spanish preposition mistakes}}.

Titles and names

When you talk about someone with a title, use the article: El señor García llega mañana, La doctora Ruiz es muy amable. When you talk to them, drop it: Buenos días, señor García.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Body parts and clothing

English uses possessives with body parts and clothes; Spanish uses the article, because the reflexive or indirect pronoun already shows whose it is:

  • Me duele la cabeza. My head hurts.
  • Se lavó las manos. She washed her hands.
  • Ponte el abrigo. Put your coat on.

Languages and countries

After hablar, aprender and estudiar, languages usually go without an article: Hablo español. As the subject, they take it: El español es fácil. Most countries take no article (México, España, Chile), but a few do or may: El Salvador (always), la India, (el) Perú, (los) Estados Unidos.

Contractions: al and del

A + el becomes al, and de + el becomes del: Voy al cine, Vengo del trabajo. The exception is when El is part of a proper name: Viajé a El Salvador.

Why this happens

Learners decide on articles by asking “specific or general?” and “countable or not?”. Spanish asks slightly different questions, so the instinct misfires in predictable places. As a translator, I see these article choices change in almost every sentence I turn from English into Spanish. The best fix is exposure: read Spanish regularly and notice where the articles fall, especially with general statements and professions.

Common mistakes

Try it yourself

  1. I love chocolate. (Me encanta el chocolate.)
  2. She’s a nurse. (Es enfermera.)
  3. Can I have another glass? (¿Me das otro vaso?)
  4. On Fridays we eat out. (Los viernes comemos fuera.)
  5. Wash your hands. (Lávate las manos.)

Articles also depend on gender: see {{link:spanish-gender-mistakes|Spanish gender mistakes}}. All mistake types in {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Add the article for general statements, days, titles and body parts. Drop it with professions after ser and before otro, medio, cien, mil. These few patterns cover most article mistakes learners make.

faq.q: Why does Spanish say me gusta el café and not me gusta café?
faq.a: Spanish uses the definite article for nouns in a general sense, so “I like coffee” is Me gusta el café.

faq.q: Do you say soy un profesor or soy profesor?
faq.a: Soy profesor. Spanish drops un with professions after ser, unless there is an adjective: Es un profesor excelente.

faq.q: Is it un otro or otro?
faq.a: Otro, never un otro: otro café, otra vez.

questions.explain: No una with professions after ser.
Otro/otra never takes an indefinite article.
Days take el and no preposition.
